plan.concept: RANSAC robustly fits a geometric model by iteratively proposing candidates from minimal random samples and counting how many data points support them.
learningObjectives: Identify how a minimal sample set (2 points) uniquely defines a candidate line model.
Explain how a distance threshold separates inlying data from outlier noise.
Understand why RANSAC is resilient to extreme outliers that would otherwise ruin standard least-squares fitting.
plan.keyInsight: Instead of trying to fit a model to all points at once—which outliers would heavily distort—RANSAC iteratively guesses models using tiny random subsets of points until it finds one that the majority of the data agrees with.

interactions.label: RANSAC Trial
interactions.effect: Selects different pairs of random points (shown in red) to generate candidate lines, shifting the line and updating which points are colored blue (inliers) or white (outliers).
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates how random sampling sometimes generates poor candidate models (when outliers are picked) and sometimes generates excellent candidate models (when only inliers are picked).

interactions.label: Inlier Threshold
interactions.effect: Controls the width of the tolerance band around the candidate line, changing points between blue (inliers within threshold) and white (outliers outside threshold).
interactions.teaches: Shows how the threshold parameter determines what level of noise is tolerated before a point is discarded as an outlier.

demo_steps.title: Proposing a Bad Candidate
demo_steps.narration: Look at the two red points selected in this iteration. Because one of the randomly chosen points is an outlier, the resulting candidate line is highly skewed and gets very low support (only 2 or 3 inliers).
demo_steps.focus: The poorly aligned line passing through one outlier and one inlier point, leaving most true inliers colored white.

demo_steps.title: Finding the Winning Model
demo_steps.narration: Now look at Trial 5, where both randomly selected red points happen to be true inliers. This candidate line aligns perfectly with the main cluster, yielding a consensus of 8 inliers (shown in blue).
demo_steps.focus: The red line aligned with the diagonal cluster, colored blue, and labeled with '8 inliers'.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting the Tolerance
demo_steps.narration: Slide the Inlier Threshold down. Notice how tightening the tolerance turns nearby blue points into white outliers, reducing our consensus support because we are being too strict with natural sensor noise.
demo_steps.focus: Blue points near the line turning white as the threshold tolerance band narrows.

demo_steps.title: Ignoring Extreme Outliers
demo_steps.narration: Finally, look at the isolated white points on the right. Because they lie far outside our inlier threshold, RANSAC completely ignores them, protecting our final model from being skewed by corrupt data.
demo_steps.focus: The isolated white points on the far right which have zero influence on the position of the red line.

plan.reconstructionNotes: An interactive scatter plot with an X and Y axis. A set of roughly 12 data points is plotted: a main diagonal line cluster with some noise, and a few isolated extreme outlier points on the right. Users can slide through 'Trials' where different pairs of points turn red, and a line is drawn through them. Points within a threshold distance of this line are colored blue (inliers) and others white (outliers). An annotation dynamically counts the number of inliers (e.g., '8 inliers').
